segments.voice: Yesterday, in Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum, the fast: it clears space and turns each pang into a bell. A new week begins, and the night goes on.
screen: `THE FAST: HUNGER AS A BELL.` · `A NEW WEEK, THE SAME NIGHT.`

segments.voice: A little before two in the morning, in a temple courtyard. The crowd that pushed through the gates at sunset has thinned. A child sleeps across her grandmother's lap. A man in a shawl keeps nodding, catching himself, nodding again. Even the drummer looks tired. Hours like this decide whether a vigil is kept or quietly given up. Then somebody near the shrine starts a new song, loud, with a call everyone knows how to answer. Heads lift. The man in the shawl sits up and sings.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `THE HARDEST HOUR.` → `SOMEBODY STARTS A SONG.`

segments.voice: Keeping awake on this night is called jagarana, the vigil. It gives the night its character, and it's easy to misread as a test of endurance. Look at how it's done. First, together. In temples, singing, chanting and rounds of worship come one after another, so there's always something to wake into. You keep yourself awake, and the person next to you, and they keep you. Second, on purpose. People stay up all night for many reasons. The vigil asks you to stay up toward something, attention pointed at Shiva, hour after hour. Third, it points past the night. The Katha Upanishad has a call that fits this hour: arise, awake, go to the great teachers and learn. It warns that the path is as sharp as a razor's edge. That wakefulness isn't about eyelids. But staying awake on this one night is a way of rehearsing the other kind. So the courtyard at two in the morning is a small picture of the whole teaching. Everyone is tired. Nobody is awake by their own strength alone. And what lifts the heads isn't a scolding. It's a song someone was willing to start. Sometimes, in the hard hour, the lesson isn't to stay awake. It's to be the one who starts the song.
screen: `JAGARANA: THE VIGIL.` · `KEPT AWAKE TOGETHER.` · `AWAKE TOWARD SOMETHING.` · `ARISE, AWAKE, AND LEARN.` · then, large: `BE THE ONE WHO STARTS THE SONG.`

segments.voice: Sit a little straighter than usual, eyes just slightly open and resting on a spot in front of you, and when the mind starts to drift or dull, the way heads nod at two in the morning, don't scold yourself. Lift: straighten the back, take one fuller breath, and come back, because every lift is a small vigil. If you pray, you can let Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, be the song that lifts you.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Lesson three: jagarana, the vigil, wakefulness kept together and pointed toward Shiva, a rehearsal for waking up.
Your line: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Nobody stays awake alone. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus who keep the jagarana stay awake through the night, in temples or at home, with bhajans, chanting of Om Namah Shivaya, and rounds of worship of the linga until dawn.

chat.says: Is the Shivaratri vigil basically a contest to see who stays up longest?
options: No: it's kept together and on purpose, awake toward Shiva, not just awake.
Yes: whoever lasts till dawn without help has kept the vigil best.
No: it's kept alone, in total silence, so no one keeps you awake.
